title: A Systematic Literature Review: Present Bias versus Financial Literacy as Determinants of Savings Behavior Among Entrepreneurs
authors: Aquino, Efren James S.; Sealmoy, Ruth R.; Mandap, Oliver R.
tldr: Present bias is a stronger predictor of poor entrepreneurial savings than financial literacy, which only improves savings when combined with high self-control.
problem_and_motivation: Despite widespread financial literacy training, entrepreneurs frequently fail to save even when financially knowledgeable. The knowledge–action gap suggests behavioral barriers like present bias may be more influential than knowledge alone. Few studies systematically compare the relative predictive power of financial literacy versus present bias on entrepreneurial savings.
approach: Systematic literature review following PRISMA 2020 guidelines.
Search across Google Scholar, Scopus, Web of Science with Boolean keywords.
20 studies met criteria from 18 journals across 6 years.
Thematic synthesis comparing financial literacy and present bias effects.
Dual-pathway theoretical framework: Financial Literacy Pathway vs Behavioral Bias Pathway.
findings: num: 9 of 20 studies used regression analysis (37%), most common method.
num: 3 studies used SEM (17%) for mediating factor models.
num: 14 studies (78%) used primary data collection.
num: 11 studies (56%) focused on Asian contexts.
num: Distribution peaked in 2022 with 5 articles.
Financial literacy's impact is conditional—often negligible without self-control.
Present bias consistently leads to impulsive spending and reduced savings.
Behavioral factors frequently override financial knowledge.
Self-control moderates financial literacy's effect on savings.
Integrated interventions combining education with behavioral design are essential.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: The review establishes that present bias—not financial literacy—is the stronger predictor of poor entrepreneurial savings. Financial literacy matters but mainly when combined with high self-control. Without it, knowledge often fails to translate into action. The dual-pathway framework contrasts Financial Literacy Pathway (knowledge → confidence → savings) with Behavioral Bias Pathway (present bias → low self-control → impulsive spending → reduced savings). The evidence strongly supports the Behavioral Bias Pathway, suggesting integrated interventions combining education with behavioral tools are essential.
